resolutions.question: WINSORIZATION PARTITION: 'We winsorize all variables at the 1st and 99th percentiles' -- is this pooled across the full 1997-2015 sample? By fiscal year? By industry-year? What do Bates 2009 and Opler 1999 use? Does the paper's Table 1 report pre-winsorize or post-winsorize summary statistics?
resolutions.paper_says: Section 3.3, p.536: 'We winsorize all variables at the 1st and 99th percentiles to minimize the influence of outliers. Table 1 provides summary statistics of the key variables used in this study. We report the mean, standard deviation, 25th percentile, median, and 75th percentile.' The two sentences are adjacent in the same paragraph, with the winsorization statement immediately preceding the Table 1 summary-statistics statement -- the natural reading is that Table 1 reports POST-winsorize stats. The paper is silent on partition (pooled vs by-year vs by-industry-year).
resolutions.inherited_convention: Bates et al. (2009), JF 2009, and Opler et al. (1999), JFE 1999, both winsorize at the 1st/99th percentiles POOLED across their full estimation sample (no by-year or by-industry partition). This is the dominant convention in the post-1999 corporate-cash-holdings literature; the modal Stata implementation is 'winsor2 var, cuts(1 99)' without a by() option.
resolutions.resolved_answer: Winsorize pooled across the full regression sample (all 56,646 firm-years, all 1997-2015, all FF49 industries combined). Compute the 1st and 99th percentile of each variable on the post-filter sample, replace values below the 1st percentile with the 1st-percentile value, and replace values above the 99th percentile with the 99th-percentile value. Table 1 then reports these winsorized values. Do NOT partition by year or industry unless robustness checks find that the published coefficients only reproduce under a partitioned scheme.

resolutions.question: WINSORIZATION ORDERING: Does winsorization happen BEFORE or AFTER the sample filters (SIC drop, AT>0 drop)? Cited templates often say: 'All variables are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles of their empirical distributions' -- what distribution? Full Compustat, or post-filter sample?
resolutions.paper_says: Section 3.1 lists the sample filters first, ending with 'This yields a final sample of 56,646 firm-year observations.' Section 3.3 then describes variable construction, ending with the winsorization sentence. The narrative order is filter -> construct -> winsorize, which is the standard reading.
resolutions.inherited_convention: Bates 2009 and Opler 1999 both apply winsorization to the post-filter sample (i.e., AFTER SIC exclusions and AT>0 cuts), not to raw Compustat. This is implicit but uniformly followed: the 1st/99th percentile cutoffs are computed on the same sample that enters the regression.
resolutions.resolved_answer: Winsorize AFTER all sample filters have been applied. The 1st/99th percentile cutoffs are computed on the 56,646-observation regression panel, not on raw Compustat. Operational sequence: (a) apply all SIC, AT, and missing-value filters; (b) construct all variables; (c) compute 1%/99% percentile cutoffs on each variable using the resulting panel; (d) clip values to those cutoffs.

resolutions.question: MISSING-VALUE HANDLING FOR CONTROLS: Only Dividend Payer has explicit missing -> 0. For R&D, Acquisitions, CapEx, Book Lev, MTB, CF, NWC: does the paper drop or impute? Search the paper, footnotes, appendix, and any online appendix for any statement. Then check Bates 2009 for each variable's treatment.
resolutions.paper_says: Section 3.3 and Appendix A Table A1: only Dividend Paying Firms(0/1) has an explicit 'set to zero if missing' instruction. The paper is silent on missing-value handling for all other controls. Section 3.3: 'We follow the literature (Bates et al., 2009; Opler et al., 1999) in our empirical testing and control for several variables that affect firm cash policy.'
resolutions.inherited_convention: Bates 2009 (JF 2009, Section II): 'We require that firms have positive assets (Compustat data item #6) and positive sales (data item #12) to be included in a given year.' Bates 2009 sets R&D = 0 when missing (XRD is missing for ~40-50% of Compustat firm-years; dropping would leave too few observations). Bates 2009 sets Acquisitions = 0 when missing (firms that don't acquire have AQC missing). The Boasiako-Keefe Table 1 Panel A reports Acquisition Expenditure with p25 = 0 and median = 0, which is empirically achievable only if missing AQC was imputed to zero -- if missing AQC observations had been dropped, the zero-mass would not exceed 50% of the resulting sample. This is independent empirical confirmation that Boasiako-Keefe inherits the Bates 2009 zero-imputation convention.
resolutions.resolved_answer: (a) Dividend Paying Firms(0/1): set to 0 if missing (paper-explicit). (b) R&D Expenditure: set XRD = 0 if missing (Bates 2009 convention, inherited). (c) Acquisition Expenditure: set AQC = 0 if missing (Bates 2009 convention, inherited; confirmed by Table 1 Panel A's >50% zero-mass). (d) Capital Expenditure: drop if CAPX missing (Bates 2009 keeps; missingness is rare). (e) Book Leverage: drop if DLC or DLTT missing (no zero-imputation convention). (f) Market-to-book: drop if any of CEQ, CSHO, PRCC_F missing. (g) Cash Flow: drop if any component missing. (h) Net Working Capital: drop if any of ACT, LCT, CHE, AT missing. (i) Industry Cash Flow Volatility: drop firm-year if industry has fewer than 3 years of CF observations in the rolling window (paper-explicit).

resolutions.question: AT TIMING ON DENOMINATORS: Cash, CapEx, AcqExp, R&D use 'at the beginning of the year.' Book Leverage, Market-to-book, Cash Flow, NWC use 'to book assets' / 'to total book assets' with NO timing qualifier. Is this contemporaneous AT_t or lagged AT_{t-1}? Which do Bates 2009 and Opler 1999 use for each?
resolutions.paper_says: Appendix A Table A1: Cash, External Debt Financing, External Equity Financing, Capital Expenditure, Acquisition Expenditure, and R&D Expenditure all carry the explicit phrase 'at the beginning of the year' on the denominator. Book Leverage, Market-to-book, Cash Flow, and Net Working Capital carry only 'to book assets' / 'to total book assets' / 'to net assets' with no timing qualifier.
resolutions.inherited_convention: Bates 2009 (NBER WP 12534 verbatim): 'Capital expenditures to assets. We measure capital expenditures as the ratio of capital expenditures (#128) to book assets (#6).' No 'beginning of year' qualifier. 'Leverage. We measure leverage using the debt/assets ratio, defined as (long-term debt plus debt in current liabilities) / book value of assets.' No timing qualifier. 'Market to book is measured as: (book value of total assets - book value of equity + market value of equity)/book value of total assets.' No timing qualifier. Bates 2009 uses CONTEMPORANEOUS AT (data #6) throughout -- 'book assets' without qualifier means current-fiscal-year-end AT. Where Boasiako-Keefe deviates from Bates 2009 by adding 'at the beginning of the year' (Cash, CapEx, AcqExp, R&D), they are signaling a meaningful change to lagged AT. Where Boasiako-Keefe is silent (Book Lev, MTB, Cash Flow, NWC), they revert to the Bates 2009 default = contemporaneous AT.
resolutions.resolved_answer: Use AT_{t-1} (lagged / beginning-of-year) for: Cash, Capital Expenditure, Acquisition Expenditure, R&D Expenditure, External Debt Financing, External Equity Financing. Use AT_t (contemporaneous / fiscal-year-end) for: Book Leverage, Market-to-book, Cash Flow, Net Working Capital. The explicit/silent split in Table A1 mirrors the standard flow-vs-stock convention in the cash-holdings literature: flow variables (CapEx, AcqExp, R&D) and the headline cash ratio are scaled by lagged AT to avoid the simultaneity that would arise if the current-year flow affected current-year AT; stock variables (Book Lev, MTB, NWC) are scaled by contemporaneous AT because both numerator and denominator are point-in-time fiscal-year-end snapshots. Cash Flow's grouping with stocks here is the one mild surprise but follows Bates 2009 verbatim.

resolutions.question: INDUSTRY CF VOL -- EXACT ROLLING WINDOW SPECIFICATION: 'previous 10 years, at least 3 years of observations required.' For fiscal year t, does the window include years [t-10, t-1] or [t-9, t]? If CF data starts in 1987 and the sample starts in 1997, does every firm-year have a full 10-year lookback? If not, how are early years handled?
resolutions.paper_says: Appendix A Table A1: 'Standard deviation of industry average cash flows for the previous 10 years; at least 3 years of observations required.' The phrase 'previous 10 years' is most naturally read as the 10 years preceding year t -- i.e., the window [t-10, t-1], a backward-looking window exclusive of the current year. The 'at least 3 years of observations required' clause allows the variable to be computed when the industry has fewer than 10 historical observations, as long as at least 3 are available.
resolutions.inherited_convention: Bates 2009 (NBER WP verbatim): 'Industry sigma is the mean of standard deviations of cash flow/assets over 10 years for firms in the same industry as defined by two-digit SIC code.' Bates uses two-digit SIC, NOT FF49 -- Boasiako-Keefe deviates from Bates here by using FF49 (footnote 5). The 10-year window is the standard convention; Bates 2009 does not explicitly say whether it includes year t or excludes it, but the dominant implementation in subsequent literature is the backward-looking [t-10, t-1] window (computed on lagged data so that the volatility measure is in the firm's information set when it sets cash at time t).
resolutions.resolved_answer: For each firm-year (i, t) in FF49 industry j: (a) compute each Compustat firm-year's Cash Flow ratio (per ambiguity-4 timing); (b) for each industry-year (j, s), compute the cross-sectional MEAN of Cash Flow across firms in industry j in year s -- call this CF_bar_{j,s}; (c) for the regression firm-year (i, t), compute the standard deviation of CF_bar_{j,s} for s in [t-10, t-1] (10 backward-looking years, exclusive of t); (d) if fewer than 3 of those 10 industry-years have observations, set Industry Cash Flow Volatility = missing and drop firm-year (i, t). With the sample beginning in 1997 and CRSP/Compustat going back to ~1962, every firm-year from 1997 onward should have a full 10-year lookback for the established FF49 industries; only newly-defined or sparse industries in early years would bind on the 3-year minimum.

resolutions.question: ESTIMATION SOFTWARE AND IMPLEMENTATION: Does the paper name any software (Stata, SAS, R)? Any command (reghdfe, areg, xtreg, plm)? The paper reports heteroskedasticity-consistent SE from state-clustered covariance. What finite-sample correction does the standard cash-holdings literature use for clustered SE with ~50 clusters?
resolutions.paper_says: The paper does not name any software package, command, or estimation routine. Table 2 notes report only: 'standard errors are clustered by state' (Columns 1-4); 'standard errors are two-way clustered by state and year' (Column 5); 'Heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors are reported in parentheses.'
resolutions.inherited_convention: Standard cash-holdings literature, including Bates 2009 and Francis et al. (2014) (which Boasiako-Keefe cites as the model specification template -- 'Our model setup mirrors that of Francis et al. (2014)', Section 3.2), is implemented in Stata. The modal commands are: 'reghdfe Cash DisclosureLaw controls, absorb(state year industry) cluster(state)' for the absorb-everything specification, or 'areg Cash DisclosureLaw controls i.state i.year, absorb(industry) cluster(state)' for the older areg approach. Both apply the Stata default cluster-robust SE adjustment: (G/(G-1)) * ((N-1)/(N-K)) where G = number of clusters and K = number of parameters. With 50 clusters (US states + DC + territories) the Liang-Zeger asymptotic approximation is generally adequate; no bootstrap correction is needed.
resolutions.resolved_answer: Most likely Stata, most likely reghdfe (or areg). Apply cluster-robust SE at the state level with Stata's default DOF correction: vce(cluster state) in modern syntax, or cluster(state) in legacy. With ~50 state clusters the small-cluster wild-bootstrap correction (Cameron-Gelbach-Miller 2008) is not strictly needed for inference but would not change point estimates. Sign that the paper used reghdfe specifically: the reported Adj R^2 = 0.4939 for Column (1) includes the absorbed industry / state FE variance; reghdfe by default reports this combined R^2, whereas areg reports only the residual-on-projected R^2 (different number). Confirming whether the reported value matches reghdfe's default would identify the package.

resolutions.question: FIXED-EFFECTS ABSORPTION METHOD: Column (1) says year + industry + state FE. Does the paper absorb these as dummy variables, or use a within-transformation (demeaning)? In Stata's areg, industry is absorbed and state dummies are explicit; in reghdfe, all three are absorbed. Does the paper's Adj R^2 formula tell us which?
resolutions.paper_says: Paper is silent. Table 2 notes simply list 'Year fixed effects Yes', 'Industry fixed effects Yes', 'State fixed effects Yes' for Column (1) and report 'Adj. R^2 0.4939'. No specification of demeaning vs. dummy inclusion.
resolutions.inherited_convention: Identification: under OLS, dummy-variable inclusion vs. within-transformation produce IDENTICAL point estimates and IDENTICAL state-clustered SE. The choice affects only computational speed and the reported R^2 / Adj R^2 (which depend on whether absorbed-FE variance is included in the numerator). The Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem guarantees the equivalence. Therefore the choice is operationally irrelevant for replication of the coefficient on Disclosure Law(0/1).
resolutions.resolved_answer: Use either reghdfe (absorb(year industry state)) or explicit dummy variables for all three FE sets -- they produce identical point estimates and identical state-clustered SE. To replicate the exact reported Adj R^2 = 0.4939, use reghdfe defaults (which include absorbed-FE variance in R^2). If reproducing in R, use fixest::feols(Cash ~ DisclosureLaw + controls | year + industry + state, cluster = ~state) which matches reghdfe's R^2 conventions. Identification result: ambiguity does NOT block coefficient replication.
resolutions.confidence: high (on irrelevance for coefficient replication); low (on the exact package the authors used)

resolutions.question: STATE ASSIGNMENT FOR TREATMENT: 'focusing on the states in which firms are headquartered' -- is HQ state from Compustat's STATE field (current-year filing address), or from the CRSP/Compustat merged database header? Does the paper use the same state for all years (first-appearance state) or time-varying state? The treatment dummy switches at the state-year level -- what happens if a firm relocates?
resolutions.paper_says: Section 3.2, p.535: 'focusing on the states in which firms are headquartered is a conservative approach, since it essentially downward biases beta in Equation (1), which should result in an underestimation of our treatment effect. In other words, firms that are partly pre-exposed to a data breach disclosure law will have a weaker reaction when a similar law is passed in their home state.' Paper does not specify the data source for the HQ state field, and does not address firm relocations.
resolutions.inherited_convention: Standard cash-holdings literature uses Compustat's STATE field (the company's current HQ address as reported in the most recent filing). Compustat's STATE field is NOT historical -- it shows the firm's current HQ as of the latest annual filing, applied retroactively to all firm-years in the database. This is a known limitation: if a firm relocated from CA to TX in 2010, Compustat will show TX for ALL years 1997-2015. To use truly time-varying HQ state, researchers must collect HQ history from 10-K filings (Bill McDonald's historical HQ dataset is the standard source). The paper's silence on this is consistent with using Compustat's static STATE -- the easier and more common approach.
resolutions.resolved_answer: Most likely Compustat STATE field, applied statically (each firm has one HQ state for the entire sample period, determined by current Compustat filing). Firms that relocated are mis-assigned for pre-relocation years. This is a known sample-design limitation, not a paper error, and is explicitly acknowledged by the authors as 'a conservative approach' that 'downward biases' beta -- i.e., they accept the bias. For replication: extract STATE from the Compustat header (gvkey-level, time-invariant in the typical extract) and apply it uniformly to all firm-years for that gvkey. Do NOT use the McDonald historical HQ panel unless explicitly trying to extend the paper.

resolutions.question: TREATMENT TIMING -- Y+1 PRECISION: 'switches to one the year after the focal state passed the disclosure law.' If a state passes a law in June 2005, does Disclosure Law = 1 for fyear=2006? Or fyear=2005 (if passage-year+1 means calendar-year+1 and fyear 2005 starts after passage)? Or does 'year after' mean the next calendar year regardless of fiscal year? What does the paper's cited NCSL source use as the passage date (effective date or enactment date)?
resolutions.paper_says: Section 3.2, p.535: 'Disclosure Law(0/1)_{s,t} is a dummy variable that switches to one the year after the focal state passed the disclosure law.' Table A1: '1 for periods after the enactment of the state-level data breach notification laws, and 0 otherwise.' Footnote 3, p.533: 'See the various state disclosure laws from the National Conference of State Legislatures, at http://www.ncsl.org/research/telecommunications-and-information-technology/security-breach-notification-laws.aspx.' The paper uses the word 'enactment' in Table A1 and 'passed' in Section 3.2; it does not specify whether passage-year is the year of enactment (when the legislature voted), or the year of effective date (when the law became operative -- typically 3-12 months after enactment).
resolutions.inherited_convention: NCSL's security-breach-notification-laws table reports BOTH the enactment date (e.g., 'enacted 2005') and the effective date (e.g., 'effective July 1, 2006'). For many states these differ by 6-12 months. The standard convention in the law-and-finance literature (Francis et al. 2014, which Boasiako-Keefe cites as the model template, and Beck et al. 2010, which they also cite) is to use the YEAR OF ENACTMENT (calendar year of legislative passage) as the passage year, and set the treatment dummy to 1 starting the FISCAL YEAR FOLLOWING enactment. So if CA enacts in 2002, Disclosure Law(0/1) = 1 for fyear 2003 onward. This is the 'one-year lag' that 'the year after' refers to in Section 3.2.
resolutions.resolved_answer: Use enactment year (calendar year the state legislature passed the law) from the NCSL table. Set Disclosure Law(0/1) = 1 for all firm-years where fyear >= enactment_year + 1, and 0 otherwise. Example: California enacted in 2002 -> Disclosure Law(0/1) = 1 for fyear in {2003, 2004, ..., 2015} for CA-headquartered firms. This convention matches Beck et al. (2010) and Francis et al. (2014), both cited by the paper as methodological templates (Section 3.2: 'Similar to previous studies (Beck et al., 2010; Francis et al., 2014), we use a difference-in-differences approach'). Do NOT use effective date; do NOT use month-of-enactment for sub-annual precision.

resolutions.question: SAMPLE CONSTRUCTION ORDER: Section 3.1 says 'This yields a final sample of 56,646 firm-year observations' AFTER the SIC+AT filters but BEFORE introducing the 11 controls. Does the 56,646 come from just SIC+AT filters, or has the panel already been merged with the disclosure law treatment variable (requiring non-missing state) and dropped firms that can't be assigned to a state? Does the paper's online appendix have an explicit sample-construction attrition table?
resolutions.paper_says: Section 3.1, p.534: 'we collect initial firm-level data from the merged Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP)/Compustat database for the period 1997-2015 ... we exclude all financial firms ... We exclude utility companies ... We further drop observations with negative or missing total book assets. This yields a final sample of 56,646 firm-year observations.' The phrase 'final sample' and the count 56,646 -- which exactly matches the N reported in Table 2 Column (1) and Table 1 Panel A -- both imply this is the regression-ready panel after ALL filters, not just SIC+AT. The Section 3.1 prose lists only the SIC+AT filters because those are the only EXPLICIT filters; the implicit filters (CRSP-link, state non-missing for treatment assignment, all controls non-missing with zero-imputation for R&D/AcqExp/Dividend) operate silently in the background.
resolutions.inherited_convention: Bates 2009 and Opler 1999 both report a single 'final sample' N at the end of Section II Data, with the implicit filters folded in: (a) CRSP/Compustat link required, (b) all regression variables non-missing (with R&D and AcqExp zero-imputed), (c) industry classification assignable. Boasiako-Keefe inherits this presentation style.
resolutions.resolved_answer: The 56,646 reflects the FULL regression-ready panel after applying: (1) period 1997-2015; (2) loc-USA-or-state-is-US-jurisdiction (so HQ state is assignable for treatment); (3) CRSP/Compustat merge (for Firm Age and treatment-time-series); (4) SIC NOT in 4900-4999 and NOT in 6000-6999; (5) AT > 0 (positive and non-missing); (6) AT_{t-1} > 0 (so beginning-of-year denominators are defined); (7) all 11 controls computable, with R&D, Acquisition Expenditure, and Dividend Paying Firms imputed to zero when missing; (8) Industry Cash Flow Volatility computable (>= 3 years of industry CF in 10-year lookback). The paper does NOT publish a step-by-step attrition table; an Online Appendix referenced in footnote 7 (https://sites.google.com/site/mockeefe/Data, with the EFM appendix PDF on Dropbox) may contain one, but Dropbox returned ROBOTS_DISALLOWED on automated fetch attempts -- it must be downloaded manually to confirm.

unresolvable: Ambiguity 1 partition (high-confidence direction toward pooled, but the paper's silence means a robustness check is needed; if pooled winsorization fails to reproduce the published coefficients within rounding, try by-year, then by-industry-year). External information needed: the Online Appendix at https://www.dropbox.com/s/anlc4amo14zkyr8/BK%20EFM%20Online%20Appendix.pdf (manual download required) likely contains the partition spec.

Ambiguity 6 software identity is genuinely unrecoverable from the paper text. The Adj R^2 = 0.4939 is consistent with both reghdfe and areg defaults but not uniquely diagnostic. Replication packages or the corresponding author (michael.keefe@vuw.ac.nz, listed in the paper's header) would be required to confirm.

Ambiguity 9 treatment-date precision: the paper does not distinguish enactment vs. effective date. For states where these dates straddle a fiscal-year boundary (e.g., enacted late 2005, effective mid-2006), the treatment-assignment year may differ by one. The paper's footnote 3 URL (NCSL) provides both dates -- replication should test both date conventions and compare the resulting beta to the reported 0.0076 to identify which the authors used.

Ambiguity 8 HQ state: Compustat STATE is static (one value per gvkey). The paper does not say whether they used Compustat STATE directly or constructed a time-varying HQ panel from 10-K filings. For most firms this does not matter (no relocation), but for the ~5-10% of firms that relocated within 1997-2015 it does. No way to resolve from paper text alone.
